Answer: 3M's GAAP operating income margin fell 1.7 percentage points in FY2022, from 20.8% to 19.1% (operating income $6,539M on net sales of $34,229M vs. $7,369M on $35,355M) — 3M's FY2022 10-K, pp. 20–21, 27, 48. Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M (it is a diversified manufacturer and 3M itself presents a margin bridge), but the GAAP figure is heavily distorted in 2022 by non-recurring special items, so the adjusted bridge better reflects underlying performance. Drivers, per 3M's own bridge (pp. 20–21, 27): Underlying (excluding special items), margin fell 1.4 pts from 22.2% to 20.8%: - Raw material/inflation impact: (2.4) pts — continued inflationary pressure from year-on-year increases in raw material and logistics costs driven by geopolitical, logistics and disruptive events unbalancing the global supply chain (also cited in cost of sales, which rose to 56.2% of sales from 53.2%). - Organic growth/productivity and other: +1.0 pt, composed of: • (0.3) pt from declines in disposable respirator demand year-on-year; • +1.3 pt net from remaining organic growth/productivity — benefits from strong pricing, spending discipline and 2021 restructuring actions, offset by manufacturing headwinds from global supply chain challenges, geopolitical impacts of the Russia/Ukraine conflict and ongoing COVID-related challenges in China, increased investments in growth/productivity/sustainability, and the loss of the prior-year Q2 2021 $91M pre-tax Brazilian Supreme Court social-tax benefit. - ERP deployment investments also pressured cost of sales, SG&A and R&D. Special items, net (1.7) pts (from +1.4 pts in 2021 to (1.7) pts in 2022): - Net costs for significant litigation (6.7) pts — including the Q2 2022 ~$1.2 billion pre-tax charge for steps toward resolving Combat Arms Earplugs litigation and additional commitments for PFAS matters at the Zwijndrecht, Belgium site; - Gain on business divestitures +8.0 pts ($2,724M, mainly the September 2022 Food Safety split-off); - PFAS manufacturing exit costs (2.4) pts; Russia exit charges (0.3) pts; divestiture costs (0.2) pts; divestiture-related restructuring (0.1) pt. By line item (p. 27): cost of sales +3.0 pts of sales; SG&A +6.1 pts (litigation, PFAS/Russia exit impairments, divestiture restructuring, growth investment, partly offset by restructuring benefits and cost management); R&D (0.2) pt; goodwill impairment +0.8 pt; gain on divestitures (8.0) pts. Divestitures (lost income/stranded costs, Food Safety and Aearo deconsolidation) and a stronger U.S. dollar hurt sales and earnings but had no direct margin-pt impact in the bridge (FX decreased operating income ~$271M year-on-year).
Final: Answer: 3M's GAAP operating income margin fell 1.7 percentage points in FY2022, from 20.8% to 19.1% (operating income $6,539M on net sales of $34,229M vs. $7,369M on $35,355M) — 3M's FY2022 10-K, pp. 20–21, 27, 48. Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M (it is a diversified manufacturer and 3M itself presents a margin bridge), but the GAAP figure is heavily distorted in 2022 by non-recurring special items, so the adjusted bridge better reflects underlying performance. Answer: Quick ratio at June 30, 2023 (Q2 FY2023) ≈ **0.85x** — (cash and equivalents $4,258M + current marketable securities $56M + accounts receivable–net $4,947M = $9,261M) ÷ total current liabilities $10,936M (3M 10-Q, p.5). (On the alternative "current assets less inventories and prepaids" definition, it is $9,800M/$10,936M ≈ 0.90x; both are down slightly from 0.88x at December 31, 2022.) Interpretation — yes, 3M's liquidity profile is reasonably healthy, but the quick ratio alone understates it: - A sub-1.0x quick ratio mainly reflects that $3,033M of short-term borrowings/current portion of long-term debt (including $1.8B of commercial paper outstanding at 6/30/23) sit in current liabilities. These are routinely rolled over rather than repaid from liquid assets; 3M states its "primary short-term liquidity needs are met through cash on hand and U.S. commercial paper issuances" and that it "maintains a strong liquidity profile" (p.70). - Backup liquidity: an undrawn $4.25B five-year revolving credit facility (May 2023, expandable to $5.25B, replacing the prior $3.0B and $1.25B facilities), plus proven capital-markets access and staggered maturities; $2,784M of operating cash flow in the first six months; net debt of $11,650M vs. total debt $15,987M (pp.70–71). - Caveats: cash is concentrated offshore (~$3.2B of the $4.3B held by foreign subsidiaries vs. ~$1.1B in the U.S.), and the Q2 PFAS charge (~$10.3B pre-tax, largely in long-term "other liabilities," which jumped to $14,651M from $5,615M) plus credit downgrades/watch (A2 negative; A– CreditWatch negative) are pressures the quick ratio does not capture, and working capital fell $0.3B to $4,818M. So the quick ratio is a relevant but limited gauge here — because a large share of 3M's current liabilities is refinanced commercial paper/current maturities rather than obligations to be settled from cash and receivables, the ~0.85x reading does not indicate unhealthy liquidity.

Answer: Roughly 9.5 times (Total cost of sales $10,069M ÷ year-end inventory $1,055M ≈ 9.5x, ~38 days of inventory; using average inventory of ($1,055M + $604M)/2 = $830M gives ≈12.1x). However, conventional inventory turnover is not really meaningful for AES: it is a power generation/utility company that sells electricity and capacity, not inventory. Its inventory is only fuel and other raw materials ($733M) plus operational spare parts and supplies ($322M) held for its own use (AES_2022_10K, Note 2, p.149; accounting policy p.140), and its "cost of sales" line is a broad operating-cost caption that includes electricity and fuel purchases, O&M, depreciation and amortization, bad debt, and G&A/support costs rather than a pure cost of goods sold (p.86). Thus the fuel inventory consumed is not the driver of cost of sales, so the computed ratio overstates/misrepresents "inventory turns."
Final: Answer: Roughly 9.5 times (Total cost of sales $10,069M ÷ year-end inventory $1,055M ≈ 9.5x, ~38 days of inventory; using average inventory of ($1,055M + $604M)/2 = $830M gives ≈12.1x). However, conventional inventory turnover is not really meaningful for AES: it is a power generation/utility company that sells electricity and capacity, not inventory. Its inventory is only fuel and other raw materials ($733M) plus operational spare parts and supplies ($322M) held for its own use (AES_2022_10K, Note 2, p.149; accounting policy p.140), and its "cost of sales" line is a broad operating-cost caption that includes electricity and fuel purchases, O&M, depreciation and amortization, bad debt, and G&A/support costs rather than a pure cost of goods sold (p.86). Thus the fuel inventory consumed is not the driver of cost of sales, so the computed ratio overstates/misrepresents "inventory turns."

**Evidence (Amcor plc, FY2023 Form 10-K, Consolidated Balance Sheets, p. 52, $ in millions):** | | June 30, 2023 | June 30, 2022 | |---|---|---| | Cash and cash equivalents | 689 | 775 | | Trade receivables, net | 1,875 | 1,935 | | Quick assets | 2,564 | 2,710 | | Total current liabilities | 4,476 | 5,103 | | **Quick ratio** | **0.57x** | **0.53x** | - FY2023: (689 + 1,875) / 4,476 = 0.573 - FY2022: (775 + 1,935) / 5,103 = 0.531 → improvement of ~0.04x (+7.9%) - The improvement came almost entirely from the liability side: total current liabilities fell $627M (trade payables 3,073 → 2,690 on inventory-reduction/moderated purchasing, short-term debt 136 → 80, accrued employee costs 471 → 396, plus $65M of Russian liabilities held for sale derecognized), which more than offset the decline in cash + receivables. (Even adding the $75M of FY2022 cash classified as held for sale, FY2022 would be 0.55x — still a year-over-year improvement.) **Is this the metric an analyst would use?** It's computable, but the quick ratio is a secondary/atypical lens for Amcor. It is a capital-intensive, investment-grade global packaging manufacturer that deliberately runs minimal balance-sheet cash and holds essentially no marketable securities (its liquidity documentation for FY2023 cites $1.261B of operating cash flow, $3.8B of committed revolving facilities of which $2.5B was drawn, i.e. **$1.3B undrawn**, plus commercial-paper access, and a net debt/Adjusted EBITDA covenant capped at 3.9x — see pp. 39-40, 86). A ratio below 1.0x here reflects a working-capital-efficient, revolver-backed liquidity model rather than a solvency problem, so analysts typically emphasize working capital / cash conversion, the current ratio, free cash flow coverage, net debt/EBITDA and committed facility availability instead. Answer: Improved — Amcor's quick ratio rose from about 0.53x in FY2022 to about 0.57x in FY2023 (a gain of ~0.04x, ~8%), driven by lower current liabilities ($5,103M → $4,476M, mainly trade payables) outweighing lower cash and receivables ($2,710M → $2,564M). Note that the quick ratio is not the metric an analyst would typically emphasize for Amcor: it is a capital-intensive, investment-grade industrial that intentionally holds little cash and no meaningful marketable securities, funding liquidity through operating cash flow and $1.3B of undrawn committed revolvers/commercial paper, so sub-1.0x quick ratios reflect an efficient working-capital model rather than weak liquidity (AMCOR_2023_10-K, pp. 39-40, 52, 86).
Final: **Evidence (Amcor plc, FY2023 Form 10-K, Consolidated Balance Sheets, p. 52, $ in millions):** | | June 30, 2023 | June 30, 2022 | |---|---|---| | Cash and cash equivalents | 689 | 775 | | Trade receivables, net | 1,875 | 1,935 | | Quick assets | 2,564 | 2,710 | | Total current liabilities | 4,476 | 5,103 | | **Quick ratio** | **0.57x** | **0.53x** | - FY2023: (689 + 1,875) / 4,476 = 0.573 - FY2022: (775 + 1,935) / 5,103 = 0.531 → improvement of ~0.04x (+7.9%) - The improvement came almost entirely from the liability side: total current liabilities fell $627M (trade payables 3,073 → 2,690 on inventory-reduction/moderated purchasing, short-term debt 136 → 80, accrued employee costs 471 → 396, plus $65M of Russian liabilities held for sale derecognized), which more than offset the decline in cash + receivables. (Even adding the $75M of FY2022 cash classified as held for sale, FY2022 would be 0.55x — still a year-over-year improvement.) **Is this the metric an analyst would use?** It's computable, but the quick ratio is a secondary/atypical lens for Amcor. It is a capital-intensive, investment-grade global packaging manufacturer that deliberately runs minimal balance-sheet cash and holds essentially no marketable securities (its liquidity documentation for FY2023 cites $1.261B of operating cash flow, $3.8B of committed revolving facilities of which $2.5B was drawn, i.e. **$1.3B undrawn**, plus commercial-paper access, and a net debt/Adjusted EBITDA covenant capped at 3.9x — see pp. 39-40, 86). A ratio below 1.0x here reflects a working-capital-efficient, revolver-backed liquidity model rather than a solvency problem, so analysts typically emphasize working capital / cash conversion, the current ratio, free cash flow coverage, net debt/EBITDA and committed facility availability instead. Answer: Improved — Amcor's quick ratio rose from about 0.53x in FY2022 to about 0.57x in FY2023 (a gain of ~0.04x, ~8%), driven by lower current liabilities ($5,103M → $4,476M, mainly trade payables) outweighing lower cash and receivables ($2,710M → $2,564M). Note that the quick ratio is not the metric an analyst would typically emphasize for Amcor: it is a capital-intensive, investment-grade industrial that intentionally holds little cash and no meaningful marketable securities, funding liquidity through operating cash flow and $1.3B of undrawn committed revolvers/commercial paper, so sub-1.0x quick ratios reflect an efficient working-capital model rather than weak liquidity (AMCOR_2023_10-K, pp. 39-40, 52, 86).

Answer: No—on a reported basis, Amcor’s gross margin did not improve in FY2023. Gross profit was $2,725 million on net sales of $14,694 million, a 18.5% gross margin, down from $2,820 million and 19.4% in FY2022, and down from 21.2% in FY2021. Gross margin is a limited/distorted metric for Amcor in this period because it largely passes through higher raw-material costs: $776 million of FY2023 net sales reflected raw-material cost pass-throughs, increasing both sales and cost of sales without adding gross profit. Management said the reported gross-margin decline was mainly due to this pass-through effect and disposed operations. Excluding currency and disposed/ceased operations, gross profit increased $56 million due to favorable operating-cost performance. A more useful assessment combines gross profit dollars with adjusted EBIT/EBITDA margin; Amcor’s adjusted EBIT margin declined from 11.7% to 10.9%, although management said about 90 basis points of that decline came from the raw-material pass-through denominator effect.
Final: Answer: No—on a reported basis, Amcor’s gross margin did not improve in FY2023. Gross profit was $2,725 million on net sales of $14,694 million, a 18.5% gross margin, down from $2,820 million and 19.4% in FY2022, and down from 21.2% in FY2021. Gross margin is a limited/distorted metric for Amcor in this period because it largely passes through higher raw-material costs: $776 million of FY2023 net sales reflected raw-material cost pass-throughs, increasing both sales and cost of sales without adding gross profit. Management said the reported gross-margin decline was mainly due to this pass-through effect and disposed operations. Excluding currency and disposed/ceased operations, gross profit increased $56 million due to favorable operating-cost performance. A more useful assessment combines gross profit dollars with adjusted EBIT/EBITDA margin; Amcor’s adjusted EBIT margin declined from 11.7% to 10.9%, although management said about 90 basis points of that decline came from the raw-material pass-through denominator effect.

Answer: As of the Q2 FY2023 close (December 31, 2022), Amcor's restructuring liability is an accrual of remaining cash obligations under its restructuring plans — principally the restructuring activities arising from the Russia‑Ukraine conflict (the exit/orderly sale of its three Russian manufacturing facilities, completed December 23, 2022, and the suspended Ukraine site), together with residual amounts from the 2019 Bemis Integration Plan, and it relates primarily to the Flexibles reportable segment. Its purpose is to fund the wind‑down/exit costs of those actions, and it is composed of employee-related costs (severance/termination benefits) of $81 million, fixed asset-related costs of $2 million, and other costs of $10 million, for a total restructuring liability of $93 million (down from $118 million at June 30, 2022, after $2 million of net charges to earnings, $25 million of cash paid and $2 million of reversals of unused amounts). The accrual is recorded on the balance sheet within other current liabilities and other non-current liabilities, with the majority expected to be paid within the next twelve months (Amcor 10‑Q for the quarter ended December 31, 2022, Notes 3, 4, 5 and 6, pages 12–15).
Final: Answer: As of the Q2 FY2023 close (December 31, 2022), Amcor's restructuring liability is an accrual of remaining cash obligations under its restructuring plans — principally the restructuring activities arising from the Russia‑Ukraine conflict (the exit/orderly sale of its three Russian manufacturing facilities, completed December 23, 2022, and the suspended Ukraine site), together with residual amounts from the 2019 Bemis Integration Plan, and it relates primarily to the Flexibles reportable segment. Its purpose is to fund the wind‑down/exit costs of those actions, and it is composed of employee-related costs (severance/termination benefits) of $81 million, fixed asset-related costs of $2 million, and other costs of $10 million, for a total restructuring liability of $93 million (down from $118 million at June 30, 2022, after $2 million of net charges to earnings, $25 million of cash paid and $2 million of reversals of unused amounts). The accrual is recorded on the balance sheet within other current liabilities and other non-current liabilities, with the majority expected to be paid within the next twelve months (Amcor 10‑Q for the quarter ended December 31, 2022, Notes 3, 4, 5 and 6, pages 12–15).

Q: Does AMD have a reasonably healthy liquidity profile based on its quick ratio for FY22? If the quick ratio is not relevant to measure liquidity, please state that and explain why.
⭐ GOLD (ground truth): Yes. The quick ratio is 1.57, calculated as (cash and cash equivalents+Short term investments+Accounts receivable, net+receivables from related parties)/ (current liabilities).

Q: What are the major products and services that AMD sells as of FY22?
⭐ GOLD (ground truth): AMD sells server microprocessors (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs), data processing units (DPUs), Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and Adaptive System-on-Chip (SoC) products for data centers; CPUs, accelerated processing units (APUs) that integrate CPUs and GPUs, and chipsets for desktop and notebook personal computers; discrete GPUs, and semi-custom SoC products and development services; and embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products.

Answer: AMD's FY2022 net revenue rose 44% to $23.6 billion (from $16.4 billion in 2021), driven by: (1) a 64% increase in Data Center revenue ($6.0B) primarily due to higher sales of EPYC server processors; (2) a 21% increase in Gaming revenue ($6.8B) from higher semi-custom product sales on greater demand for gaming console SoCs, partially offset by lower gaming graphics sales on softer consumer demand amid weakened macroeconomic conditions in 2H22; (3) a significant increase in Embedded revenue ($4.6B vs. $246M) driven by the inclusion of Xilinx embedded product sales following the February 2022 Xilinx acquisition; partially offset by (4) a 10% decrease in Client revenue ($6.2B) due to a 24% decline in unit shipments from challenging PC market conditions and a significant inventory correction across the PC supply chain in 2H22, somewhat mitigated by a 19% higher average selling price from a richer Ryzen mobile mix. (Source: AMD FY2022 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, pp. 43, 48–49)
Final: Answer: AMD's FY2022 net revenue rose 44% to $23.6 billion (from $16.4 billion in 2021), driven by: (1) a 64% increase in Data Center revenue ($6.0B) primarily due to higher sales of EPYC server processors; (2) a 21% increase in Gaming revenue ($6.8B) from higher semi-custom product sales on greater demand for gaming console SoCs, partially offset by lower gaming graphics sales on softer consumer demand amid weakened macroeconomic conditions in 2H22; (3) a significant increase in Embedded revenue ($4.6B vs. $246M) driven by the inclusion of Xilinx embedded product sales following the February 2022 Xilinx acquisition; partially offset by (4) a 10% decrease in Client revenue ($6.2B) due to a 24% decline in unit shipments from challenging PC market conditions and a significant inventory correction across the PC supply chain in 2H22, somewhat mitigated by a 19% higher average selling price from a richer Ryzen mobile mix. (Source: AMD FY2022 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, pp. 43, 48–49)

Yes — AMD's FY2022 Form 10-K discloses customer concentration in multiple places. - **Business (Item 1, "Customers," p.17):** "One customer accounted for 16% of our consolidated net revenue for the year ended December 31, 2022. Sales to this customer consisted of sales of products from our Gaming segment. A loss of this customer would have a material adverse effect on our business." - **Note 10 – Concentrations of Credit Risk (p.91):** "One customer accounted for approximately 18% of the total consolidated accounts receivable balance as of December 31, 2022" (versus two customers at ~20% and ~15% as of December 25, 2021). AMD added that credit risk is limited because a large, geographically diverse customer base dilutes trade credit risk, and the receivables do not represent a significant credit risk. - **Risk factors (p.23, p.27):** "The loss of a significant customer may have a material adverse effect on us," noting dependence on "a small number of customers for a substantial portion of our business." No single-customer revenue concentration disclosure for a second customer, and the concentration disclosed is receivables-based (18%) plus revenue-based (16%) for one customer. Answer: Yes. In FY22 AMD reported customer concentration: one customer accounted for 16% of consolidated net revenue for the year ended December 31, 2022 (Gaming segment products, AMD 2022 10-K p.17), and the same-type disclosure in Note 10 – Concentrations of Credit Risk showed one customer at approximately 18% of total consolidated accounts receivable as of December 31, 2022 (vs. two customers at 20% and 15% at December 25, 2021) (p.91).

Answer: No — American Water Works had **negative working capital** at FY2022 year-end. Per the FY2022 10-K Consolidated Balance Sheets (page 81–82, Dec. 31, 2022), total current assets were **$1,250 million** and total current liabilities were **$2,811 million**, giving working capital of **–$1,561 million** (current ratio ≈ 0.44x). The deficit is largely due to $1,175 million of short-term debt (commercial paper) plus $281 million current maturities of long-term debt. The company itself confirms this in the risk factors (page 38): "As of December 31, 2022, our aggregate long-term and short-term debt balance (including preferred stock with mandatory redemption requirements) was $12.4 billion, and our working capital (defined as current assets less current liabilities) was in a deficit position." Working capital is not a very meaningful metric for this regulated utility: its assets are overwhelmingly long-lived property, plant and equipment ($23,223 million net PP&E vs. only $1,250 million current assets), it has steady, regulator-approved cash collections from customers, and it deliberately funds short-term needs through its commercial paper program/revolving credit facility ($2.60 billion CP and a $2.75 billion revolver, both increased in October 2022) rather than by holding large current asset balances. A persistent working-capital deficit is therefore normal and not a liquidity red flag — the company states it "utilized existing sources of liquidity, such as current cash balances, cash flows from operations and borrowings under our commercial paper program, to meet our short-term liquidity requirements" and believes those sources are sufficient for the foreseeable future.

Summary of findings: **FY2023** (ended Jan 28, 2023) — BESTBUY_2023_10K, Note 2 "Acquisitions" (p.51) lists only the two fiscal 2022 deals; the investing section (p.42) shows "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired — $0" in fiscal 2023. No acquisitions completed. **FY2022** (ended Jan 29, 2022) — BESTBUY_2022_10K (p.52–53) / BESTBUY_2023_10K (p.51): - **Current Health Ltd.** — care-at-home technology platform, all outstanding shares acquired Nov 2, 2021 for **$389M net cash**, incl. $351M goodwill assigned to Best Buy Health (Domestic segment / Services revenue). - **Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture** — direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture, acquired Nov 4, 2021 for **$79M net cash**, incl. $47M goodwill (Domestic reporting unit / Other revenue). - Total $468M cash used, matching the FY2023 10-K cash flow line. **FY2021** (ended Jan 30, 2021) — BESTBUY_2021_10K (p.44) shows "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired — $0" for fiscal 2021 (vs. $145M in FY2020 for CST/BioSensics and $787M in FY2019 for GreatCall); its Acquisitions note covers only those prior-year deals. No acquisitions completed. Answer: Best Buy completed **no acquisitions in FY2023 or FY2021**; its only major acquisitions in this three-year window were in **FY2022**: (1) **Current Health Ltd.**, a care-at-home/remote patient monitoring technology platform, acquired November 2, 2021 for **$389 million net cash** ($351 million goodwill to the Best Buy Health reporting unit, Domestic segment/Services revenue), and (2) **Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture**, a direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture company, acquired November 4, 2021 for **$79 million net cash** ($47 million goodwill to the Best Buy Domestic reporting unit, Other revenue) — totaling **$468 million** of "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired" in the FY2022 cash flow statement. (Sources: BESTBUY_2022_10K pp.4, 52–53; BESTBUY_2023_10K pp.29, 42, 51; BESTBUY_2021_10K pp.4, 44, 55.) For context outside this window, the FY2021 10-K's acquisition note covers only prior-year deals: Critical Signal Technologies ($125M, May 2019) and BioSensics ($20M, Aug 2019) in FY2020, and GreatCall ($787M, Oct 2018) in FY2019.
Final: I have sufficient evidence. Summary of findings: **FY2023** (ended Jan 28, 2023) — BESTBUY_2023_10K, Note 2 "Acquisitions" (p.51) lists only the two fiscal 2022 deals; the investing section (p.42) shows "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired — $0" in fiscal 2023. No acquisitions completed. **FY2022** (ended Jan 29, 2022) — BESTBUY_2022_10K (p.52–53) / BESTBUY_2023_10K (p.51): - **Current Health Ltd.** — care-at-home technology platform, all outstanding shares acquired Nov 2, 2021 for **$389M net cash**, incl. $351M goodwill assigned to Best Buy Health (Domestic segment / Services revenue). - **Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture** — direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture, acquired Nov 4, 2021 for **$79M net cash**, incl. $47M goodwill (Domestic reporting unit / Other revenue). - Total $468M cash used, matching the FY2023 10-K cash flow line. **FY2021** (ended Jan 30, 2021) — BESTBUY_2021_10K (p.44) shows "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired — $0" for fiscal 2021 (vs. $145M in FY2020 for CST/BioSensics and $787M in FY2019 for GreatCall); its Acquisitions note covers only those prior-year deals. No acquisitions completed. Answer: Best Buy completed **no acquisitions in FY2023 or FY2021**; its only major acquisitions in this three-year window were in **FY2022**: (1) **Current Health Ltd.**, a care-at-home/remote patient monitoring technology platform, acquired November 2, 2021 for **$389 million net cash** ($351 million goodwill to the Best Buy Health reporting unit, Domestic segment/Services revenue), and (2) **Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture**, a direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture company, acquired November 4, 2021 for **$79 million net cash** ($47 million goodwill to the Best Buy Domestic reporting unit, Other revenue) — totaling **$468 million** of "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired" in the FY2022 cash flow statement. (Sources: BESTBUY_2022_10K pp.4, 52–53; BESTBUY_2023_10K pp.29, 42, 51; BESTBUY_2021_10K pp.4, 44, 55.) Answer: Yes — in its FY2022 Form 10-K (Item 3 and Note 21 "Legal Proceedings," printed pages 108–109), Boeing disclosed that various legal proceedings, claims and U.S. government inquiries/investigations are pending, and while it generally believes such matters will not have a material effect on its financial position, results of operations or cash flows, it called out two ongoing matters for which it "cannot reasonably estimate a range of loss": 1. **737 MAX crash litigation (Lion Air Flight 610, Oct. 29, 2018; Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, Mar. 10, 2019)** — multiple legal actions remain pending. Related resolutions already recorded: the 2021 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice (resolving the DOJ investigation into the FAA's 737 MAX evaluation); a shareholder derivative settlement under which Boeing received $219 million in Q2 2022; and the September 2022 SEC settlement of the 737 MAX investigation, which produced a $200 million earnings charge (civil penalty paid in October 2022). Remaining lawsuits related to the accidents/737 MAX are not reasonably estimable. 2. **Embraer arbitration** — Boeing's 2020 termination of the 2019 agreements to acquire an 80% stake in Embraer's commercial aircraft/services operations for $4,200 million (plus the C-390 Millennium JV) is disputed by Embraer and is in arbitration, expected to conclude in late 2023 or early 2024; no range of loss is reasonably estimable. Boeing also noted that government proceedings could involve claims for fines, penalties, compensatory/treble damages, restitution or forfeitures, and could theoretically result in suspension/debarment from government contracts or loss of export privileges; its risk factors state an adverse resolution of litigation could have a material impact.
Final: Answer: Yes — in its FY2022 Form 10-K (Item 3 and Note 21 "Legal Proceedings," printed pages 108–109), Boeing disclosed that various legal proceedings, claims and U.S. government inquiries/investigations are pending, and while it generally believes such matters will not have a material effect on its financial position, results of operations or cash flows, it called out two ongoing matters for which it "cannot reasonably estimate a range of loss": 1. **737 MAX crash litigation (Lion Air Flight 610, Oct. 29, 2018; Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, Mar. 10, 2019)** — multiple legal actions remain pending. Related resolutions already recorded: the 2021 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice (resolving the DOJ investigation into the FAA's 737 MAX evaluation); a shareholder derivative settlement under which Boeing received $219 million in Q2 2022; and the September 2022 SEC settlement of the 737 MAX investigation, which produced a $200 million earnings charge (civil penalty paid in October 2022). Remaining lawsuits related to the accidents/737 MAX are not reasonably estimable. 2. **Embraer arbitration** — Boeing's 2020 termination of the 2019 agreements to acquire an 80% stake in Embraer's commercial aircraft/services operations for $4,200 million (plus the C-390 Millennium JV) is disputed by Embraer and is in arbitration, expected to conclude in late 2023 or early 2024; no range of loss is reasonably estimable. Boeing also noted that government proceedings could involve claims for fines, penalties, compensatory/treble damages, restitution or forfeitures, and could theoretically result in suspension/debarment from government contracts or loss of export privileges; its risk factors state an adverse resolution of litigation could have a material impact.

Answer: Boeing’s implied gross margin improved only marginally in FY2022—about 5.3% ($66,608M revenues less $63,106M cost of sales = $3,502M) vs. 4.8% in FY2021 and -9.8% in FY2020 (10-K, pp. 28, 55)—but gross margin is not a highly meaningful standalone metric for Boeing. Its cost of sales and margins are driven by commercial aircraft program accounting and long-term-contract estimates, and FY2022 results included large estimate-driven losses/catch-up adjustments, especially fixed-price defense development programs; consequently, even with slightly better gross margin, GAAP operating margin worsened to -5.3% from -4.7% and core operating margin worsened to -7.0% from -6.5% (10-K, pp. 24–25, 50).
Final: Answer: Boeing’s implied gross margin improved only marginally in FY2022—about 5.3% ($66,608M revenues less $63,106M cost of sales = $3,502M) vs. 4.8% in FY2021 and -9.8% in FY2020 (10-K, pp. 28, 55)—but gross margin is not a highly meaningful standalone metric for Boeing. Its cost of sales and margins are driven by commercial aircraft program accounting and long-term-contract estimates, and FY2022 results included large estimate-driven losses/catch-up adjustments, especially fixed-price defense development programs; consequently, even with slightly better gross margin, GAAP operating margin worsened to -5.3% from -4.7% and core operating margin worsened to -7.0% from -6.5% (10-K, pp. 24–25, 50).

Boeing's effective tax rate fell sharply from FY2021 to FY2022, moving from a positive double-digit rate to a negative rate. - **FY2022: (0.6)%** — income tax expense of $31 million on a pre-tax loss of $5,022 million - **FY2021: 14.7%** (per the Note 4 rate reconciliation; the MD&A summary table shows 14.8%) — an income tax benefit of $743 million on a pre-tax loss of $5,033 million That is a decline of roughly **15.3–15.4 percentage points**. The key drivers in the reconciliation: the valuation allowance impact grew to (23.9)% in 2022 from (10.2)% in 2021 (allowance rose from $2,423M to $3,162M), partially offset by R&D credits (4.1% vs 3.8%), state taxes (1.8% vs 1.9%), non-U.S. activity ((1.3)% vs (0.9)%), CARES Act ((0.1)% vs 0.1%) and other adjustments ((2.4)% vs (0.8)%). Because Boeing had pre-tax losses in both years, a negative effective rate in 2022 means it recorded a small tax *expense* despite a loss, reflecting the valuation allowance against deferred tax assets. Source: Boeing FY2022 10-K, Note 4 – Income Taxes (pp. 76–77) and MD&A "Consolidated Results of Operations" (p. 24). Answer: FY2022 effective tax rate was (0.6)%, down about 15.3 percentage points from FY2021's 14.7% (14.8% as shown in MD&A).

Q: Is CVS Health a capital-intensive business based on FY2022 data?
⭐ GOLD (ground truth): Yes, CVS Health requires an extensive asset base to operate, which is evident from its ROA of only 1.82% in 2022 and 3.39% in 2021, though it should be noted that a significant portion of this asset base is goodwill, and CVS's fixed assets/total assets ratio is on the lower side of 5.6%.

{"queries": ["Legal and Regulatory Proceedings opioids antitrust", "loss contingencies accrual material", "state attorneys general subpoena civil investigative demand"], "filters": {"company": "", "year": -1, "filing_type": "", "document_id": "CVSHEALTH_2022_10K"}, "prose_hits": [{"document_id": "CVSHEALTH_2022_10K", "company": "Cvshealth", "year": 2022, "filing_type": "10-K", "page": 1, "section": "", "passage_id": "p:CVSHEALTH_2022_10K:page:1:chunk:381", "start": 723900, "end": 726100, "text": "ion and Investigations The Company is named as a defendant in a number of lawsuits and is subject to a number of investigations concerning its PBM practices. The Company is facing multiple lawsuits, including by state Attorneys General, governmental subdivisions and several putative class actions, regarding drug pricing and its rebate arrangements with drug manufacturers. These complaints, brought by a number of different types of plaintiffs under a variety of legal theories, generally allege that rebate agreements between the drug manufacturers and PBMs caused inflated prices for certain drug products. The Company is defending itself against these claims. The Company has also received subpoenas, civil investigative demands (“CIDs”), and other requests for documents and information from, and is being investigated by, the FTC and Attorneys General of several states and the District of Columbia regarding its PBM practices, including pricing and rebates. Inventories Inventories are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value determined by the first-in, first-out method. Intangible Assets and Goodwill The authoritative literature on U.S. GAAP requires that goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite lives be assessed annually for impairment. The Company completed its annual impairment test for 2022 in the fiscal fourth quarter. Future impairment tests will be performed annually in the fiscal fourth quarter, or sooner if warranted. Purchased in-process research and development is accounted for as an indefinite lived intangible asset until the underlying project is completed, at which point the intangible asset will be accounted for as a definite lived intangible asset. If warranted the purchased in-process research and development could be written off or partially impaired depending on the underlying program. Intangible assets that have finite useful lives continue to be amortized over their useful lives, and are reviewed for impairment when warranted by economic conditions. See Note 5 for further details on Intangible Assets and Goodwill. Financial Instruments As required by U.S. GAAP, all derivative instruments are recorded on the balance sheet at fair value. Fair value is the exit price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability. Fair value is a market-based measurement determined using assumptions that market participants would use in pricing an asset or liability. The authoritative literature establishes a three-level hierarchy to prioritize the inputs used in measuring fair value, with Level 1 having the highest priority and Level 3 having the lowest. In response to these concerns, the Company has a long-standing policy of pricing products responsibly. For the period 2012 - 2022, in the U.S., the weighted average compound annual growth rate of the Company’s net price increases for healthcare products (prescription and over-the-counter drugs, hospital and professional products) was below the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI). The Company operates in certain countries where the economic conditions continue to present significant challenges. The Company continues to monitor these situations and take appropriate actions. Inflation rates continue to have an effect on worldwide economies and, consequently, on the way companies operate. The Company has accounted for operations in Argentina and Venezuela as highly inflationary, as the prior three-year cumulative inflation rate surpassed 100%. Beginning in the fiscal second quarter of 2022, the Company accounted for operations in Turkey as highly inflationary, as the prior three-year cumulative inflation rate surpassed 100%. This did not have a material impact to the Company's results in the period. In the face of increasing costs, the Company strives to maintain its profit margins through cost reduction programs, productivity improvements and periodic price increases. Russia-Ukraine War Although the long-term implications of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine are difficult to predict at this time, the financial impact of the conflict in the fiscal 2022, including accounts receivable or inventory reserves, was not material. As of both the fiscal years ending January 1, 2023 and January 2, 2022, the business of the Company’s Ukraine subsidiaries represented less than 1% of the Company’s consolidated assets and revenues. Answer: approximately $92.73 per share Evidence (JPMorgan Chase 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2021): - Consolidated balance sheet: Total stockholders' equity = $280,714 million (includes $31,563 million preferred stock), with total liabilities of $3,408,622 million already ahead of equity holders. - Cover page: 3,027,128,112 common shares outstanding as of March 31, 2021. - $280,714M ÷ 3,027,128,112 shares ≈ $92.73 per share. Note: If preferred holders ($31,563M) were paid first out of the liquidation proceeds, the residual for common shareholders would be about ($280,714M − $31,563M) ÷ 3,027,128,112 ≈ $82.31 per share.

Inventories Inventories are stated at average cost, subject to the lower of cost or market. Cost includes materials, labor, and manufacturing overhead related to the purchase and production of inventories. We regularly review inventory quantities on hand, future purchase commitments with our suppliers, and the estimated utility of our inventory. These reviews include analysis of demand forecasts, product life cycle status, product development plans, current sales levels, pricing strategy, and component cost trends. If our review indicates a reduction in utility below carrying value, we reduce our inventory to a new cost basis through a charge to cost of revenue. 48 Table of Contents PART II Item 7 STATEMENT OF MANAGEMENT’S RESPONSIBILITY FOR FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Management is responsible for the preparation of the consolidated financial statements and related information that are presented in this report. The consolidated financial statements, which include amounts based on management’s estimates and judgments, have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. The Company designs and maintains accounting and internal control systems to provide reasonable assurance at reasonable cost that assets are safeguarded against loss from unauthorized use or disposition, and that the financial records are reliable for preparing consolidated financial statements and maintaining accountability for assets. These systems are augmented by written policies, an organizational structure providing division of responsibilities, careful selection and training of qualified personnel, and a program of internal audits. The Company engaged Deloitte & Touche LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, to audit and render an opinion on the consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). The Board of Directors, through its Audit Committee, consisting solely of independent directors of the Company, meets periodically with management, internal auditors, and our independent registered public accounting firm to ensure that each is meeting its responsibilities and to discuss matters concerning internal controls and financial reporting. NOTE 14 — RISK MANAGEMENT AND DERIVATIVES The Company is exposed to global market risks, including the effect of changes in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates, and uses derivatives to manage financialexposures that occur in the normal course of business. The Company does not hold or issue derivatives for trading or speculative purposes. The Company may elect to designate certain derivatives as hedging instruments under U.S. GAAP. The Company formally documents all relationships between designatedhedging instruments and hedged items as well as its risk management objectives and strategies for undertaking hedge transactions. This process includes linking all derivatives designated as hedges to either recognized assets or liabilities or forecasted transactions and assessing, both at inception and on an ongoing basis, theeffectiveness of the hedging relationships. The majority of derivatives outstanding as of May 31, 2021, are designated as foreign currency cash flow hedges, primarily for Euro/U.S. Dollar, British Pound/ Euro, ChineseYuan/U.S. Dollar and Japanese Yen/U.S. Dollar currency pairs. The loss models incorporate various portfolio attributes, as well as macroeconomic factors such as forecasted trends in unemployment, retail e-commerce sales, and household disposable income. The forecasted macroeconomic factors are sourced externally, using a single scenario to reflect the economic conditions applicable to a particular period. Management also includes qualitative adjustments that incorporate incremental information not captured in the expected credit loss models. The principal considerations for our determination that performing procedures relating to the allowance for loans receivable is a critical audit matter are (i) the high degree of auditor subjectivity and effort in performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence relating to certain models which apply macroeconomic forecasts to estimate expected credit losses; and (ii) the audit effort involved in the use of professionals with specialized skill and knowledge. Addressing the matter involved performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence in connection with forming our overall opinion on the consolidated financial statements. These procedures included testing the effectiveness of controls relating to the allowance for loans receivable, including controls over certain models which apply macroeconomic forecasts to estimate expected credit losses. These procedures also included, among others, the involvement of professionals with specialized skill and knowledge to assist in testing management’s process for estimating the allowance for loans receivable. Testing management’s process included (i) evaluating the appropriateness of the methodology and certain models; (ii) testing the completeness and accuracy of certain data used in the estimate; and (iii) evaluating the reasonableness of management’s application of macroeconomic forecasts to estimate expected credit losses. /s/ PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP San Jose, California February 9, 2023 We have served as the Company’s auditor since 2000. 60 Table of Contents PayPal Holdings, Inc. PART I Item 1. Business. When used in this report, the terms “we,” “us,” “our,” “PepsiCo” and the “Company” mean PepsiCo, Inc. and its consolidated subsidiaries, collectively. Certain terms used in this Annual Report on Form 10-K are defined in the Glossary included in Item 7. of this report. Company Overview We were incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. We are a leading global beverage and convenient food company with a complementary portfolio of brands, including Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker and SodaStream. Through our operations, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers and other third parties, we make, market, distribute and sell a wide variety of beverages and convenient foods, serving customers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories. Our Operations We are organized into seven reportable segments (also referred to as divisions), as follows: 1) Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), which includes our branded convenient food businesses in the United States and Canada; 2) Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), which includes our branded convenient food businesses, such as cereal, rice, pasta and other branded food, in the United States and Canada; 3) PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), which includes our beverage businesses in the United States and Canada; 4) Latin America (LatAm), which includes all of our beverage and convenient food businesses in Latin America; 5) Europe, which includes all of our beverage and convenient food businesses in Europe; 2 Table of Contents 6) Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA), which includes all of our beverage and convenient food businesses in Africa, the Middle East and South Asia; and 7) Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC), which includes all of our beverage and convenient food businesses in Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China region. Frito-Lay North America Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, FLNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods. These foods include branded dips, Cheetos cheese-flavored snacks, Doritos tortilla chips, Fritos corn chips, Lay’s potato chips, Ruffles potato chip…

Software Costs We capitalize certain computer software and software development costs incurred in connection with developing or obtaining computer software for internal use when both the preliminary project stage is completed and it is probable that the software will be used as intended. Capitalized software costs include (1) external direct costs of materials and services utilized in developing or obtaining computer software, (2) compensation and related benefits for employees who are directly associated with the software projects and (3) interest costs incurred while developing internal-use computer software. Capitalized software costs are included in property, plant and equipment on our balance sheet and amortized on a straight-line basis when placed into service over the estimated useful lives of the software, which approximate five to 10 years. Commitments and Contingencies We are subject to various claims and contingencies related to lawsuits, certain taxes and environmental matters, as well as commitments under contractual and other commercial obligations. These contributions are made in accordance with applicable tax regulations that provide for current tax deductions for our contributions and taxation to the employee only upon receipt of plan benefits. Generally, we do not fund our pension plans when our contributions would not be currently tax deductible. As our retiree medical plans are not subject to regulatory funding requirements, we generally fund these plans on a pay-as-you-go basis, although we periodically review available options to make additional contributions toward these benefits. We made a discretionary contribution of $125 million to a U.S. qualified defined benefit plan in January 2023 and expect to make an additional $125 million in the third quarter of 2023. Our pension and retiree medical plan contributions are subject to change as a result of many factors, such as changes in interest rates, deviations between actual and expected asset returns and changes in tax or other benefit laws. We regularly evaluate different opportunities to reduce risk and volatility associated with our pension and retiree medical plans. See Note 7 to our consolidated financial statements for our past and expected contributions and estimated future benefit payments. Based on the evidence, yes. Pfizer's 2019 10-K explicitly identifies a one-time gain outside its normal business operations that substantially boosted net income. **Key finding (Pfizer 2019 10-K):** - On July 31, 2019, Pfizer completed the transaction combining its Consumer Healthcare business with GSK's into the GSK Consumer Healthcare joint venture, receiving a 32% equity stake. Upon closing, Pfizer deconsolidated the business and recognized a **pre-tax gain of $8.1 billion ($5.4 billion net of tax)** in the line "(Gain) on completion of Consumer Healthcare JV transaction." - The income statement shows this $8,086 million gain, and net income attributable to Pfizer rose to $16,273 million in 2019 from $11,153 million in 2018 — the transaction gain being the dominant driver of that increase. - Pfizer lists this gain among its "certain significant items," which it defines as "substantive and/or unusual... items that, either as a result of their nature or size, would not be expected to occur as part of our normal business on a regular basis." Answer: Yes — the completion of the GSK Consumer Healthcare joint venture transaction generated an $8.1 billion pre-tax ($5.4 billion net-of-tax) gain that is explicitly categorized as a significant/unusual item "not expected to occur as part of normal business on a regular basis," substantially increasing Pfizer's 2019 net income (Source: Pfizer 2019 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Income and Notes/MD&A).

Answer: Yes — the completion of the GSK Consumer Healthcare joint venture transaction generated an $8.1 billion pre-tax ($5.4 billion net-of-tax) gain that is explicitly categorized as a significant/unusual item "not expected to occur as part of normal business on a regular basis," substantially increasing Pfizer's 2019 net income (Source: Pfizer 2019 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Income and Notes/MD&A).

Selling, general and administrative expenses Selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses increased $333.8 million, or 16.2%, to $2.4 billion in fiscal 2022 compared to $2.1 billion in fiscal 2021. As a percentage of net sales, SG&A expenses decreased 40 basis points to 23.5% in fiscal 2022 compared to 23.9% in fiscal 2021. The leverage of SG&A expenses was primarily due to: ● 80 basis points of leverage due to lower marketing expenses; and ● 20 basis points of leverage of incentive compensation due to higher sales; partially offset by ● 40 basis points of deleverage of corporate overhead primarily due to strategic investments; and ● 20 basis points of deleverage of store payroll and benefits due to wage investments. {"document_id": "WALMART_2018_10K", "page_start": 1, "page_end": 1, "start": 225500, "end": 228600, "text": "imitations of Internal Control over Financia l ReportingA company's internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and thepreparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal control over financialreporting includes tho se policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactionsand dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financialstatements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance withauthorizations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorizedacquisition, use, or disposition o f the company's assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.Because of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation ofeffectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance withthe policies or procedur es may deteriorate./s/ Ernst & Young LLP Rogers, Arkansas March 30, 2018 54 Walmart Inc.
